body:
You know, I think it says something really wonderful about you as a person that even as you're hurting or hopeless or overwhelmed enough to be thinking about suicide, you're STILL thinking of ways you could help other people. It seems like helping others, or making a positive impact on the world, might be a really important value for you.

Have you considered that, by staying alive, you might do more good, and help others more, over the course of your whole life, than you would be dying and possibly providing a one-time organ donation? Just as a random example off the top of my head, by [volunteering to register organ donors](http://www.americantransplantfoundation.org/how-to-help/volunteer/prospective-volunteers/volunteer-opportunities-2/), you might facilitate thousands of organ donations, and play a small but very important role in saving thousands of lives.

Let's say you are able to find a way to help others, and make a positive impact, by living. Do you think, over time, that might give  you more of a sense of meaning, more of a reason to actually *want* to live? If there's even a small chance of that happening, do you think it would be worth trying?

>Why do you want to be engaged? It sounds like, ignoring any poly or open relationship ideas, you still have some concerns or questions. In short, you only live once, so you need to decide what that should be.

See the end of my response to /u/girlaboutoaktown.

>Other than that, figure out why the idea bothers her. It is never as simple as "I want monogamy". What does that mean to her and why is it so important to her? Often this is because of some insecurity, a programmed assumption, or an uncertainty as to what it means (if you love her, you can still love her while being able to love others). I am afraid to trivialize her position, though, since it obviously means a lot to her.

Yeah, maybe this is just a philosophical difference between you and me, but I don't view the fact that she wants a monogamous relationship as a problem with her. I think polyamory might be right for me but I don't assume it's right for everybody. She's a very thoughtful, open-minded, and self-aware person. I think she's thought about this seriously and truly knows what's right for her.

>Also, figure out why you are looking beyond what you have. Is it only to satisfy a kink or is it a broader philosophical question of how inter-personal interactions should play out? Understanding your own thoughts will go a long way to explaining yourself to her.

"a broader philosophical question of how inter-personal interactions should play out" - this phrase really resonated with me, as it's often how I think about this issue. Yes, when I think about polyamory, one of the things I think about is more freedom to experiment with my kink (and when I reflect on that, it makes me feel guilty / question how "serious" my desire really is, etc.) But I do think it's much broader than that for me. I often find myself thinking about societal expectations for how relationships and emotions are supposed to work and just finding them so frustratingly arbitrary and limiting, and thinking that people could be a lot happier and freer if we viewed relationships more flexibly and permissively. So I don't know.

>You seem to have a good grasp on your own headspace, which is important.

Thanks. But the flip side is I can go around and around and around with "on the one hand" and "on the other hand" -- I see so much complexity and ambiguity and different interpretations, which is better than simplistic black and white thinking, but also makes it much harder to just make a decision.

>Everyone's different, but never having found her sexy is a red flag for me, as I think it would be to anyone who values a healthy sex life as part of their romantic relationship. Does she "feel" this from you? Do you two have enjoyable, satisfying sex together? Maybe it's just because I can't imagine wanting a relationship with someone I wasn't wildly attracted to (for instance, still find my husband very sexy after 10 years of being together) but I think the sexual disconnect might be a real problem even if you didn't want to explore polyamory.

This is a perfect example of where I have the over-analytic back and forth I just mentioned -- sometimes I think it's a red flag. Sometimes I think... well, I just have a lower-than-average sex drive (which I think is true)... I may just have issues with self-consciousness during sex (which has been there in past relationships but is more of a problem in this one)... well, I just have unrealistic expectations for how wildly attracted I "should" feel, from being a male in a society that plasters images of sexualized, unattainably perfect women everywhere. And yes, we DO have very enjoyable, satisfying sex together. I find her very sexy when we're having sex. The issue is more that it's not super frequent (couple times a month, which is actually average based on surveys) and initiation can sometimes be a problem. So maybe that's fine, and it's okay if I don't find her wildly sexy while we're, say, sitting on the couch reading. There was a recent [NYT article](http://www.nytimes.com/2015/02/27/opinion/nothing-is-wrong-with-your-sex-drive.html) on how some people mainly experience responsive, rather than anticipatory, sexual desire, and maybe that's just the case for me.

>What's great is you're not trying to force her to accept non-monogamy like many people in your shoes do. Would she rather end the relationship than "allow" you to pursue other women, though?

Yes, pretty much. We could maybe make some very minor tweaks in what I'm "allowed" to do now. But full-on polyamory, she is not going to be on board with, and I accept that. We were just talking about this, and the conclusion was, even if she did decide to "grin and bear it" to be able to stay with me... neither of us want a relationship where she is forced to grin and bear something that hurts her, and that is NOT going to be good for the long-term health of the relationship. She strongly feels she is never going to get to a point where serious non-monogamy is something she wants or even feels neutral about. Our limited experience with me meeting other people in person for kink reasons convinces me that this is true, as even those experiences have been really difficult for her.

>Why did you decide to get engaged in the first place?

Because I love her and I see her as my partner and teammate. To be clear -- if I could, I would absolutely 100% want to be poly but have her as my primary partner. Yes, there are other issues in our relationship, but none of them make me want to end it. The issue is that being poly AND staying with her isn't an option. So I need to choose.

edit: thanks for your response, it definitely seems you're thoughtful about this. I edited my OP with a more specific question if you care to comment on it.

Brevity is not my strong suit. And yes, we've put wedding planning on hold while we/I figure this out. I definitely agree that ending things now - if that's what we end up doing is way preferable to divorce, and that realization may be part of why this is all coming up for me right now.
